title: POC scoping: capacity & autoscale - Polaris Systems
summary: Discovery/POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscale for a 6-week POC. Discussed success criteria (p95 latency and throughput), workload profile (chat + single-turn generation), reserved GPU recommendations with burst strategy to shared capacity, fallback policies to smaller models/hosted pool, benchmark plan, and timeline. Action items: pricing/quote, benchmark script, security pack, and scheduling a 2-day benchmark run in staging.
transcript:
[00:00] Chris (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — I'm Chris, account exec at Redwood.
[00:08] Liam (Head of ML): Hi all, Liam here. we're evaluating Redwood for inference for our assistant product.
[00:15] Priya (Infra): Priya, infra lead. we'll be owning deployment and network.
[00:22] Maya (SE): Maya, I'm the solutions engineer, I'll drive the bench and scoping.
[00:27] Ethan (Product): Ethan, product. mainly timeline and success crits.
[00:33] Sara (Security): Sara, security. SOC2 questions later.
[00:40] Chris: Great. goal for today is to scope capacity and autoscale for a 6 week POC, agree success criteria and a bench plan.
[00:51] Liam: Quick context: production traffic is a mix of short chat turns — avg 25 tokens per reply — and longer generation for summaries ~200-400 tokens. Peak concurrent users we expect for POC is ~120 concurrent requests, with typical p50 latency target 150-200 ms for short turns.
[01:18] Maya: ok that's helpful. when you say concurrent 120, is that active model requests or user sessions?
[01:24] Liam: active in-flight model requests. some are low token so much faster.
[01:29] Maya: got it. for capacity, we typically size by qps and token-per-second. a short-turn workload with 25 tokens at low temperature maps to X tokens/s. we should also factor KV cache hit-rate for chat — are you using persistent convo cache?
[01:45] Priya: currently we store session context in our DB, but for the POC we'd like Redwood to manage local KV caching if possible to save cost.
[01:54] Maya: yes we can enable prefix/K V cache. that'll hit dramatically for chat flows. hit rate assumptions are important — what do you estimate?
[02:03] Liam: probably 60% cache hit on short-turns for an initial estimate.
[02:08] Maya: ok, that helps. baseline sizing suggestion: reserve 2 GPUs (A100 equivalent) for the POC to guarantee throughput, with burst into the hosted pool up to 4 additional units for spikes. that gives a predictable baseline cost and headroom.
[02:24] Priya: so reserved 2 + burst to shared, how does burst pricing work? we need clear economics.
[02:31] Chris: we'll send a breakout in the quote. typically reserved capacity is a monthly commit; for POC we'll do time-boxed reserved hours and pay for burst at usage rates.
[02:40] Ethan: timeline thoughts? we want to start bench asap, target: staging bench in two weeks, 2 day run, then results review, then a short pilot.
[02:51] Maya: that's feasible. recommend we start with synthetic load that mirrors your split: 70% short chat, 30% long generate. we'll run 2k synthetic queries for throughput and 1000 latency samples for p95.
[03:05] Liam: what's a realistic p95 target we should aim for in the POC?
[03:09] Maya: for short turns 25 tokens, p95 under 250 ms on reserved GPUs is achievable; for long generates 200-400 tokens, p95 will be higher — we track time-per-token. if you need under 500 ms for long, we'll need more reserved capacity or smaller model variants.
[03:26] Sara: security questions — do you support SSO/SAML, KMS, and audit logs for Private? we need SOC2 artifacts.
[03:34] Chris: yes, we have SAML SSO, KMS integrations, and audit logs. for POC we can provide our security packet; for Private you get customer-managed KMS and VPC options.
[03:45] Sara: ok please share the pack.
[03:48] Maya: back to fallback policies: we recommend multilayer fallback — first, route to reserved GPUs; if queueing grows beyond SLA, automatically fallback to a smaller quantized model variant or to hosted pooled capacity in another region. also option to degrade quality by truncating context or using cached responses for repeated prompts.
[04:09] Priya: auto-routing across regions, will that hit data residency concerns?
[04:14] Chris: we'll adhere to tenancy and region constraints you set; for POC we can keep everything in us-west-2.
[04:20] Liam: we want to preserve the order of responses and avoid partials — how do you do graceful degradation?
[04:26] Maya: we implement in-flight request routing with a priority queue; if a request will breach latency SLO we'll send to the fallback tier. we'll tag requests so you can trace. also we keep event-level logs for debug.
[04:38] Ethan: benchmarks — what's your recommended script?
[04:41] Maya: we'll provide a JMeter-like harness; it will simulate concurrency, variable token lengths, and warm caches. steps: 1) cold start run, 2) warm cache run, 3) peak stress test, 4) long-tail stability run.
[04:56] Liam: do you support instrumenting token-level timing and per-route dashboards?
[05:01] Maya: yes via Redwood Console — token-level breakdown, per-model latency histograms, and cost estimates per route. we'll share access for the POC.
[05:10] Priya: what's the expected cost difference between reserved and pure hosted?
[05:15] Chris: rough rule: reserved reduces unit cost by ~30-50% depending on commit and usage; burst is charged at hosted rates which are higher. we'll include scenarios in the quote.
[05:24] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[05:26] Maya: another sizing note: quantization can cut GPU memory and increase throughput; if you can accept small quality drop we can run 4-bit quantized runs.
[05:35] Liam: curious about fallback to smaller models — do you have automatic model variant routing?
[05:40] Maya: yes we can set routing policies: latency-first sends to low-latency quantized variants; cost-first prefers cheaper models with slightly higher latency. policies are per-route.
[05:50] Ethan: how do you handle batch size variability? our app can batch multiple requests server-side but sometimes single request calls come in.
[05:58] Maya: auto-batching at runtime plus request-level batching. we also expose batching windows so you can tune latency vs throughput.
[06:08] Priya: for the POC network setup — we need a minimal VPC peering and SAML SSO integration, any infra tickets?
[06:16] Chris: we'll provide a runbook. for private you do VPC peering; for hosted POC we'll use VPC endpoints and secure egress.
[06:24] Sara: any data retention guarantees for logs and transcripts?
[06:28] Maya: you can configure retention; for POC we can set short retention, and we can anonymize logs if required.
[06:35] Liam: ok let's try to define concrete success criteria: 1) p95 latency for short turns under 250 ms, 2) p95 for long generates under 1.2s (or a clearly documented tradeoff), 3) stable throughput for 120 concurrent in-flight requests with <2% error rate, 4) benchmarks validated in our staging with reproducible scripts.
[07:00] Chris: that sounds reasonable. we'll codify those in the SOW for POC.
[07:06] Maya: benchmark metrics we'll capture: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s, GPU utilization, cache hit rates, cost per 1k tokens.
[07:18] Liam: what about failure modes — e.g., if reserved pool runs out and burst isn't available?
[07:23] Maya: fallback chain: 1) route to hosted pool in same region, 2) if unavailable, route to smaller quantized variant in a secondary region, 3) finally return cached or truncated responses with a response header indicating degradation. we also send alerts.
[07:39] Priya: do we get API flags to control fallback behavior at runtime?
[07:43] Maya: yes we expose route-level config and runtime flags via the control plane.
[07:48] Ethan: bench schedule — Maya you said two weeks to staging run?
[07:52] Maya: yes if we get test data and access. ideally we do a 2 day run, day 1 cold+warm, day 2 stress and long-tail.
[08:00] Liam: sample size for p95 measurement?
[08:03] Maya: recommend min 1k good samples per scenario; more is better for statistical confidence.
[08:09] Chris: for POC commercial terms, we'll propose a 6-week POC with 2 reserved GPUs and burst allowance; exact hours and price in the quote.
[08:18] Priya: can we limit burst to avoid surprise bills?
[08:22] Chris: yes we can set hard caps and send alerts before crossing thresholds.
[08:27] Sara: security doc please.
[08:30] Chris: will attach security pack and SOC2 report.
[08:33] Speaker 1: (agrees)
[08:36] Maya: technical detail — for quantized variants we test both 4-bit and 8-bit profiles; we'll report quality delta on your eval prompts.
[08:46] Liam: evaluation — we'll provide a small eval set of 200 prompts representing error cases.
[08:51] Maya: perfect, that will be part of the bench. we also recommended A/B test between reserved and hosted to measure deltas.
[08:59] Ethan: integration effort — what's the onboarding time for your SDKs?
[09:03] Chris: SDKs are drop-in, we have node/python examples; expect 1-2 days for basic integration.
[09:10] Priya: networking the staging — who will manage the infra to run bench harness?
[09:15] Maya: Redwood can run the harness in our staging and we can also provide scripts for you to run in your environment; recommended we run both.
[09:23] Liam: about logs and trace — we want per-request tracing down to token level for debugging.
[09:29] Maya: Console has trace hooks and you can export traces to your observability pipeline.
[09:33] Chris: let's agree next steps and owners.
[09:37] Liam: ok.
[09:39] [10:00] ACTION: CHRIS (AE) to send POC quote and security pack.
[10:05] [10:10] ACTION: MAYA (SE) to share benchmark harness and initial config template.
[10:12] [10:18] ACTION: LIAM to provide eval prompt set and traffic profile numbers by 2026-10-26.
[10:25] [10:30] Priya: we'll need a contact for VPN/VPC peering.
[10:33] Chris: that's me, I'll coordinate with infra.
[10:36] Maya: any other questions?
[10:39] Ethan: no, thanks.
[10:41] Chris: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the 2 day staging run.
[10:48] (call ends)
